facts.value: immediately upon the employee's demand; default if not paid within 24 hours after demand
facts.summary: Minnesota: when an employee is fired or laid off, final wages are due immediately upon the employee's demand; default if not paid within 24 hours after demand.
facts.evidence_quote: (a) When any employer employing labor within this state discharges an employee, the wages or commissions actually earned and unpaid at the time of the discharge are immediately due and payable upon demand of the employee. ... If the employee's earned wages and commissions are not paid within 24 hours after demand ... the employer is in default.
facts.source_publisher: Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes

facts.value: not later than the first regularly scheduled payday after the final day of employment
facts.summary: Minnesota: when an employee is quits or resigns, final wages are due not later than the first regularly scheduled payday after the final day of employment.
facts.evidence_quote: (a) When any such employee quits or resigns employment, the wages or commissions earned and unpaid at the time the employee quits or resigns shall be paid in full not later than the first regularly scheduled payday following the employee's final day of employment
facts.source_publisher: Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes
facts.notes: Further timing rules apply in some cases (see 181.14).

facts.applies_to: As listed by U.S. DOL, page updated November 5, 2026

facts.summary: Minnesota: frequencies marked in the U.S. DOL State Payday Requirements table: Semi-monthly (note 11); Monthly (note 11).
facts.source_title: State Payday Requirements (U.S. DOL Wage and Hour Division)
facts.source_publisher: U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division
facts.notes: Note 11: Minnesota. Under Minnesota statute, employers are required to pay their employees for all wages including salary, earnings and gratuities at least once every 31 days, and all commissions earned by an employee at least once every three months on a regular payday. Employees engaged in transitory employment must be paid at intervals of not more than 15 days. Employees of “public service corporations doing business within this state” are required to be paid at least semimonthly the wages earned by them within 15 days of the date of such payment, unless prevented by inevitable casualty. | DOL table last revised 2023-01-01; DOL says to consult the state labor office for official information. Confirm against current state law before relying on it.

facts.summary: Minnesota base new employer UI rate: Industry average (IndAvg).
facts.source_title: Significant Provisions of State Unemployment Insurance Laws, Effective July 2026
facts.source_publisher: U.S. Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration, Office of Unemployment Insurance
facts.notes: DOL footnote 3: min/max rates apply only to experience-rated employers and exclude surtaxes, surcharges and non-UI taxes. Footnote 4: new employer rate shown is the base rate; higher rates may apply by industry or other factors. DOL notes the report is not an official interpretation of state law. IndAvg means the new employer rate is the industry average rate; get the exact rate from the state agency. Rate basis: DOL base rate. It may exclude mandatory surcharges, fund-building rates and assessments; check the state agency or total_new_employer_rate where available.
